title: GPTs are GPTs: An Early Look at the Labor Market Impact Potential of Large Language Models
extended_summary:
This working paper examines the potential labor-market impact of large language models (LLMs), including GPT-family systems, rather than studying an educational intervention. The core question is how much of the U.S. workforce’s task content could be affected by LLMs and by software built on top of them. The authors develop a rubric for scoring task exposure and apply it to O*NET occupational task descriptions.

The paper uses two annotation sources: human raters and GPT-4 as a classifier. It evaluates 19,265 O*NET tasks and 2,087 detailed work activities, then aggregates task-level scores to occupations. Exposure is defined as the extent to which access to an LLM or LLM-powered software could reduce task completion time by at least 50% while maintaining quality. The analysis is conducted in the U.S. labor market context using O*NET and Bureau of Labor Statistics data.

The main findings are that LLMs appear broadly applicable across occupations, with stronger exposure in higher-wage, writing- and programming-intensive work and weaker exposure in manual or highly physical work. The paper also finds moderate to strong agreement between human and GPT-4 labels and reports that complementary software substantially increases estimated exposure. However, this is a conceptual/exposure-mapping paper with no student sample, no reading or literacy outcome measures, and no subgroup analysis of K-12 learners, emergent readers, multilingual learners, or students with disabilities.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-family large language model/chatbot used for text generation, classification, and other language tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a classifier in the paper's exposure rubric to annotate occupational tasks and detailed work activities for potential LLM impact, alongside human raters.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a methodological working paper about labor-market exposure measurement, not an empirical study of K-12 educational outcomes or subgroup effects. No literacy intervention, comparison group, or student-level outcome data are reported.
impact_tier_rationale: There is no measured educational impact on reading, literacy, or subgroup outcomes. The paper offers no effect sizes or outcome evidence relevant to K-12 learners.
